sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 1 튀어야 산다! 달라야 뜬다!
sents: Driving down a country road, you see field after field of brown cows.
Since these animals all look the same, you don’t pay much attention to each individual one.
Suddenly, something catches your eye, so you quickly take out your phone and snap a picture of it to share with your friends.
What could it be?
A purple cow!
Actually, a purple cow is not a real creature but a marketing concept introduced by American author Seth Godin.
He argued that the market landscape is like a field, with each company represented by a cow.
In today’s crowded market, conventional products and services are no longer enough to stand out among all the “brown cows.”
Instead, companies should offer something exceptional, unique, and even counterintuitive to draw the attention of consumers.
One representative example of a purple cow is the American shoe company TOMS.
Calling it the “one-for-one” model, TOMS promised to provide free shoes to a child in need for each pair it sold to a customer.
The company’s focus on social responsibility generated a great deal of media hype and attracted many customers hoping to make the world a better place.
If TOMS had adopted a more traditional business model, it would not have been possible to achieve such a high level of brand recognition.
This example clearly demonstrates how an unconventional approach can create a purple cow in the marketplace.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 2 어? 내가 여기 왜 왔더라?
sents: What am I here for?
You’ve just walked into the kitchen, but the purpose that sent you there has vanished.
This isn’t a sign of aging or distraction —it’s a fascinating cognitive phenomenon called the doorway effect.
Cognitive psychologist Gabriel Radvansky’s research suggests it may be related to how the human brain stores memories as distinct episodes tied to specific environments.
When we cross a spatial boundary, like a doorway, our brain naturally clears its short-term memory from the earlier space.
This neural mechanism essentially acts like a cognitive refresh button, allowing our brain to prepare for new memory creation in the novel environment.
So, if you’re watching TV in the living room and realize you need batteries for the remote, you might forget all about the batteries as soon as you enter the storage room.
So, how can you bypass the doorway effect?
To keep your memory intact, try to maintain a connection to the previous location.
In the example above, you can bring the remote with you into the storage room.
Or, before you enter the storage room, mentally picture the living room to help remind you of your task.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 3 모르면 당하는 리듬의 함정
sents: When you walk into a store, café, or service space, music is almost always present.
Calm music in a therapy room or energetic music in a sports shop feels so natural that most people barely notice it.
We usually assume that background music simply creates a certain mood.
But in reality, it can do much more than that.
Our behavior can be subtly regulated by background music, with the timing of payments, departures, and duration of stay often being shaped without conscious awareness.
One of the most powerful tools is rhythm.
Particularly in environments where efficiency is prioritized does music characterized by a steady, highly predictable rhythm tend to promote behavioral efficiency.
For this reason, such music is often used in fast-food restaurants or other places where quick turnover is important.
The regular beat can subtly push customers to finish their meals, make decisions faster, and leave sooner.
In contrast, music with less predictable rhythms demands more attention.
Because the brain cannot easily anticipate subsequent patterns, the perception of time may become less structured, leading individuals to remain longer without conscious awareness of the cause.
Another strategy is using music that is designed to be easy to ignore.
When a song is too familiar or emotionally engaging, it can compete with products for attention.
For this reason, some high-end stores deliberately choose music without clear melodies or memorable hooks, aiming to support the shopping experience rather than become the focus.
Ultimately, background music is not mere decoration but an invisible force that subtly shapes all of our behaviors.

sets.name: Unit 01 Reading 4 The Bear That Wasn’t Quite a Bear
sents: At first glance, the giant panda seems like an easy case for taxonomy.
It looks like a bear, walks like a bear, and is often called a “panda bear.”
Yet for more than a century, scientists debated where it truly belonged on the animal family tree.
The problem was that the panda looked like a bear in some ways but in other ways resembled raccoons.
As researchers examined pandas more closely, the confusion grew.
Their diet was dominated by bamboo, and they possessed a strange “thumb” that helped them grip stalks.
This thumb was not a true finger, but an enlarged wrist bone—an unusual tool for a carnivore.
Even more puzzling, giant pandas do not hibernate like most bears.
Because bamboo provides limited energy, pandas cannot build enough fat reserves to sleep through the winter.
Instead, they must stay active and adjust their location to find food.
These traits fueled arguments that giant pandas should not be placed in the same category as bears.
But as scientific techniques advanced, molecular evidence began to reveal the truth.
DNA-based studies strongly supported the idea that the giant panda is closer to bears than to raccoons, and this view gradually became the mainstream position.
Today, giant pandas are considered bears, yet they are also classified in a distinct category that reflects their unusual characteristics.
Calling it a bear is not wrong.
Still, given how distinct it is from other bears, simply calling it a “panda” may be more appropriate.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 1 그 총이 이렇게 쓰이다니!
sents: Early in the movie Zootopia, the police officer Judy uses a carrot-shaped pen, which is actually a voice recorder, to catch Nick admitting to a crime.
At first, this scene seems like just a fun moment demonstrating how cleverly Judy tricks Nick, but surprisingly, the pen plays a decisive role in defeating the villain later in the movie!
This is an example of Chekhov’s Gun.
Chekhov’s Gun is a storytelling concept introduced by the Russian playwright Anton Chekhov.
He argued that if a gun is shown hanging on the wall in the first act, it must be fired in the second or third act.
In other words, elements important to the story’s climax should be introduced earlier.
So what role does Chekhov’s Gun play in a story?
First, it ensures that every element is meaningful.

Not only does this concept prevent irrelevant details from cluttering the narrative, but it also signals to the audience that anything they notice may be significant later, which keeps the audience engaged and makes the story more immersive.
Additionally, reintroducing an element later in the story creates a satisfying payoff.
In the case of Zootopia, if the carrot-shaped pen hadn’t been introduced earlier, the audience wouldn’t have experienced the same sense of satisfaction when it appeared at the climax.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 2 불안해서 많이 못 빌려줘
sents: While a haircut usually refers to a hair salon service, in finance, it has a very different meaning related to loans.
Imagine someone applying for a $100,000 loan using their home as collateral.
The home’s current market value may be $100,000, but the bank appraises it at $80,000 and offers a loan of that same amount.
The reason the bank reduces the home’s worth is to protect itself from a sudden plunge in asset value.
In this context, a haircut describes the difference between an asset’s assigned value and its actual market value.
Haircut rates change with the economic cycle.
When asset values decline, haircut rates increase as banks seek more protection against potential losses.
If more financial institutions adopt similar measures and raise their haircuts to safeguard assets, a haircut contagion can be triggered.
As high haircut rates spread, the amount of money available for lending decreases.
Due to high haircuts, borrowers unable to get loans may sell their depreciating assets at low prices.
This can leave them incapable of paying off their debts and lead to mass bankruptcies.
The 2008 financial crisis exposed the dangerous potential of haircut contagion.
As the subprime mortgage market collapsed, financial institutions dramatically increased haircut rates, which created a severe cash shortage and froze credit markets.
Today, economists argue that these conditions were significant factors in the global economy eventually falling into a deep recession.
In order to limit contagions, some policies have been suggested.
One of them requires banks to hold more cash.
This would allow them to provide loans without having to impose high haircuts during economic downturns.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 3 다 짜고 치는 고스톱이었어
sents: Professional wrestling is a cultural phenomenon, entertaining audiences worldwide.
Behind it, there is a concept called kayfabe.
Kayfabe is a rule designed to make audiences believe that the wrestlers’ characters and interactions are real, even though they are actually fake.

The origin of the term is unclear, but some speculate that it is derived from early 20th-century carnival slang, which allowed performers to speak with each other in code to avoid breaking character in front of the audience.
Over the years, wrestlers have gone to great lengths to protect kayfabe.
One of the most extreme examples occurred in 1975, when Ric Flair and Tim Woods were involved in a plane crash.
Both were rushed to the nearest hospital, but there was another problem besides their injuries: they were supposed to be bitter rivals at all costs.
If the public had suspected that they had been traveling together like close friends, the authenticity of professional wrestling would have been in serious jeopardy.
So, despite suffering from broken ribs and a concussion, Woods checked himself out of the hospital to avoid being seen near Flair.
Thanks to his incredible commitment, kayfabe could be safely preserved, and Woods was praised as the “Man Who Saved Wrestling.”
Then in 1989, the largest wrestling organization publicly acknowledged that professional wrestling was just entertainment with scripted scenarios, making strict kayfabe unnecessary.
Nevertheless, wrestlers today still abide by kayfabe to offer immersive and thrilling experiences for fans.

sets.name: Unit 02 Reading 4 Did a Witch Really Leave This Behind?
sents: As you walk through a lush forest with sunlight streaming through the leaves, you suddenly spot something strange.
One tree branch has a thick cluster of short, spiky stems that looks like the end of a broom.
What can it be?
It’s a common plant deformity called witches’-broom!
How did this plant get such a wicked name?
In the past, people believed this was created by witches to make their flying brooms.
However, it has been discovered to be a result of insects, fungi, or viruses that interfere with the normal growth process of a tree.
In a healthy tree, a group of hormones called auxins limits the growth of small offshoots and instead focuses the tree’s energy into increasing the size of its trunk and primary branches.
But when witches’-broom forms, the opposite happens.
The production of auxins is reduced in the infected section of a tree, causing multiple offshoots to begin to grow uncontrollably in a wild, tangled mess.
While the formation of witches’-broom may make a tree less attractive, it generally has no negative effect on the tree’s health.
In fact, it plays an important ecological role in a forest.
Studies have shown that it contributes to an increase in biodiversity by providing shelter for many species of insects, birds, and small mammals.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 1 늑대는 무섭고 개는 귀여운 이유
sents: Why does a dog look friendly while a wolf appears frightening, even though they are the same species?
The answer is in their eyes.

Compared to wolves, dogs possess two highly developed facial muscles that give them their endearing appearance: the levator anguli oculi medialis (LAOM) and the retractor anguli oculi lateralis (RAOL).
The LAOM is located above the eye, near the nose, and helps raise the eyebrows.
The RAOL is near the outer corner of the eye and widens the eye by pulling it toward the ears.
Together, these muscles enable dogs to create a sad, pleading expression that appeals to human empathy.
This expression also resembles that of infants, which may promote a nurturing response from people.
In fact, one study showed that dogs in shelters who exhibit puppy dog eyes are more likely to be adopted than those who don’t.
Researchers believe that over 30,000 years of domestication, dogs evolved these traits to help them bond with their human companions emotionally, and secure consistent care and protection.
So, when your furry friends look at you, remember that the warm connection you sense in their deep eyes is not your imagination.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 2 분명 나보다 더 바보가 있을 거야
sents: Michael saw a unique baseball card for sale in a store for $500.
Although he knew that the price was too high for the card, he eventually purchased it.
His behavior can be explained by the greater fool theory.
This is a concept whereby an investor purchases an overvalued asset based on the belief that another person will buy it at a higher price.
Basically, it is similar to the hot potato game.
Let’s go back to Michael’s case.
He believed that the baseball card was in demand by collectors and one of them would be willing to pay more than he did to get their hands on it, allowing him to profit.
While it might seem like a rational investment strategy, the greater fool theory can be extremely hazardous.
Not only is the asset’s price uncertain to rise, but also the existence of a potential buyer is unpredictable.
An example that illustrates this risk is the Dutch Tulip Mania, where tulip bulbs with rare patterns were traded at unprecedented prices during the 17th century.
They were even valued higher than craftsmen’s annual incomes!
But the market for the rare tulip bulbs collapsed abruptly in 1637, inflicting massive losses on those who were still seeking greater fools.

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 3 키스할 수도, 울 수도 있어
sents: After finishing a routine full of stunning leaps and brilliant spins, figure skaters face one more challenge.
They must stand in the “kiss-and-cry” to receive their scores, with everyone watching them intently to see how they will react.
But why is it called the kiss-and-cry?
This unusual name was coined by Finnish skating official Jane Erkko in 1983.
She noticed that when skaters received their scores in the waiting area, they tended to kiss someone to celebrate or burst into tears of joy or sorrow, depending on how well they did.
When someone asked her about the area, she called it the kiss-and-cry.
Since this name was quite appropriate, it became the official terminology in figure skating.
Nowadays, the kiss-and-cry is an important part of televised competitions.
It is often decorated like a TV set, with beautiful flowers, colorful backdrops, and special lighting, while cameras are set up to capture the skaters’ reactions.
Because of the importance of the area to a skater’s public image, some even receive special training on how to create a good impression while there!
So, the next time you watch a figure skating competition, look closely at what happens when the scores are announced.
Do the skaters kiss or cry?

sets.name: Unit 03 Reading 4 The Little Box That Started It All
sents: “Take one, share one, enjoy!”
The message on these street-corner bookshelves represents more than just a book exchange.
It’s a cultural movement that brings neighbors closer through the joy of reading.
This idea began with one man’s love for his mother.
In 2009, Todd Bol wanted to honor his late mother in a special way.
Remembering how much she loved reading, he decided to share her passion for books with others in his community.
He went straight to his old garage and created a small wooden box designed to hold books.
Then he installed it in his front yard and wrote “Free Book Exchange” on it, placing a few of his mother’s books inside.
His small attempt quickly became the talk of the neighborhood.
Inspired by this, Bol developed the idea further and established a non-profit organization called Little Free Library.
Its movement spread rapidly, and more than 200,000 community bookshelves have been installed in over 120 countries around the world.
So, how do Little Free Libraries work?
Basically, you can take any book you want to read and donate any book you are willing to share.
Unlike traditional libraries, there are no membership requirements, return deadlines, or maximum borrowing limits.
These libraries are managed by volunteers, who regularly organize the bookshelves and remove damaged books.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 1 방법을 몰랐을 뿐이야
sents: On the competitive battlefield of Wall Street, the heart of America’s financial industry, would you believe that a blind analyst could succeed?
This is the inspiring story of Soon-Kyu Shin!
Born in South Korea, Shin lost his eyesight at the age of nine despite undergoing 22 surgeries to cure his eye disease.
At 15, he moved to the US to attend a special school for the blind.
Although he initially didn’t speak English, he eventually graduated from Harvard and worked at JP Morgan, a leading financial institution in the US.
Before being hired, he needed to pass a financial analyst exam.
However, there was one major obstacle: Shin wasn’t permitted to use his specialized calculator for the blind, as the exam policy prohibited the use of personal devices.
Demonstrating that where there’s a will, there’s a way, he brilliantly managed to memorize the layout of a traditional calculator and passed the test.
This triumph marked the moment when Wall Street got its first blind analyst!
When he reflected on that experience, Shin said, “It’s not that I couldn’t do it; I just hadn’t found the way yet.”

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 2 빵! 쏘는 배를 줄 테니 톡! 쏘는 물을 다오
sents: In the late 1980s, the United States and the Soviet Union were Cold War adversaries, each with an incredibly powerful naval force.
Surprisingly, one of the largest navies at the time did not belong to either nation.
In fact, it did not belong to any country —it was owned by the American beverage company Pepsi!
In 1972, Pepsi struck a deal to sell its trademark product in the Soviet Union.
But the Soviets could not pay because the ruble, their currency, was not allowed to be used internationally due to the Soviet government’s closed monetary policy.
Instead, Pepsi entered into a barter agreement to trade Pepsi-Cola for Soviet vodka.
At first, the deal was incredibly successful for both sides, but by the end of the 1980s, it was clear that the Soviets wanted Pepsi a lot more than Americans wanted vodka.
Meanwhile, protests in the US over the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan had caused vodka sales to decline.
In need of something else to offer, Soviet officials proposed trading retired vessels —17 submarines and three warships— for more Pepsi.
Pepsi gladly accepted the offer, but it soon sold all the vessels for scrap metal.
Obviously, as a competitor in the beverage industry, it had no aspirations of becoming a naval superpower.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 3 툭하면 배가 아파요
sents: For some people, consuming dairy products causes gas and bloating, while others experience intense stomachaches from eating fried foods.
Nearly 10 percent of the global population regularly suffers similar digestive symptoms brought on by Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS), a condition that affects the body’s digestive system.
Despite impacting so many people, doctors have not found a definitive cause of IBS.
One leading hypothesis blames antibiotics.
Although they are prescribed to treat bacterial infections in the body, they may also kill off beneficial gut bacteria, upsetting the balance of gut microbes necessary for healthy digestion.
Another theory suggests that this syndrome may be a product of psychological factors, including childhood trauma or mental disorders such as depression.
Due to the link between the brain and the gut, strong feelings of anxiety may cause muscles in the stomach and intestines to contract irregularly, interfering with normal digestive function.
IBS can have a distressing effect on people’s sense of well-being as the symptoms are unpredictable and challenging to control.

Fortunately, recent research suggests that people can at least manage them through diet modifications that avoid problematic foods, lifestyle changes that reduce stress, and medications that alleviate pain.

sets.name: Unit 04 Reading 4 You’ve Been Played by the Narrator
sents: When we hear a story, we naturally experience it through the storyteller’s perspective, especially when we haven’t witnessed the events firsthand.
Filmmakers sometimes take advantage of this by using an unreliable narrator— a storytelling technique in which the person telling the story misleads the audience.
But why do directors choose this technique?
One major reason is to create suspense and shocking plot twists.
In The Usual Suspects, the main character Verbal Kint, a nervous, low-level gang member who walks with a limp, narrates a complex story about a mysterious and terrifying gang leader to a detective.
As the story unfolds, the audience becomes fully immersed in his perspective.
But in the film’s final moments, his limp vanishes as he walks away, revealing that he had fabricated the entire story.
The terrifying figure he had spoken of was not someone else, but him.
This revelation leaves viewers stunned and forces them to reconsider everything they believed about the story.
Directors occasionally include unreliable narrators to give the audience insight into a character’s mindset.
In the movie Joker, the main character Arthur believes he is in a romantic relationship with his neighbor Sophie.
But it is later revealed that the relationship was nothing more than Arthur’s imagination.
By seeing the delusions that Arthur experiences, the audience experiences a mixture of sympathy and discomfort toward him, even when he commits violent acts.
In essence, this narrative technique immerses audiences in the character’s story, allowing them to form a deeper emotional connection with the character.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 1 개가 왜 거기서 나와...?
sents: On a peaceful morning in the park, you spot a couple pushing a stroller.
You look over, expecting to see a cute baby inside.
But instead, there’s a dog!
This couple exemplifies DINKWAD—Dual Income, No Kids, With a Dog.
The term describes an increasingly popular lifestyle where couples decide to forgo children and instead make pets, particularly dogs, the focus of their family life.
The concept of DINKWAD evolved from DINK, which refers to people who are employed and childless.

With their concern about the rising costs of raising children and emphasis on personal freedom, these couples choose to focus on career development and leisure activities rather than on creating a traditional family.
For DINKWADs, the addition of pets marks a shift in priorities, with dogs providing companionship and a sense of family without the long-term commitments of child-rearing.
DINKWAD couples typically have substantial assets, because both partners work and they avoid the financial burden of raising a child to adulthood.
This freedom affords them an autonomous lifestyle and allows them to invest in personal interests and experiences such as traveling.
However, this trend could result in long-term societal issues, such as declining birth rates and a shortage of young people in the workforce to support a large aging population.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 2 그 안무가 진짜였어?
sents: “One look, give them whiplash.”
In “Whiplash,” a song by the K-pop group aespa, this line means to make such a strong impression that it feels like a physical jolt.
In sync with the powerful beat, the members perform a charismatic neck movement.
Interestingly, this motion is not merely a piece of choreography incorporated to render a performance visually more dynamic.
The name whiplash actually comes from the lightning-fast lashing motion of a whip.
It is a common neck injury, typically associated these days with traffic accidents, with over a million cases reported each year in the US alone.
Should a vehicle abruptly decelerate during a collision, an individual’s neck may violently snap back and forth like a whip, thereby inducing the injury.
Its symptoms generally include neck pain and stiffness.
An injured person may also experience headaches, dizziness, neck muscle swelling, and nausea, as well as memory and vision problems.
These symptoms usually fade in a few weeks with minimal treatment, such as taking pain medications and applying ice to relieve swelling.
But in more severe cases, surgery may be necessary to repair damage to the bones or nerves in the neck, which can take months to recover from.
Automotive safety specialists assert that the optimal remedy for whiplash lies in its prevention.
They recommend setting the seat headrest as close to the head as possible.
This reduces the risk of the neck snapping back during a collision.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 3 천사를 보여 주면 천사를 그리겠소
sents: Standing before a painting, you see an anguished man staring back at you.
He is grasping his hair with both hands, as if he has the weight of the world on his shoulders.
This work is Gustave Courbet’s The Desperate Man, a self-portrait that reflects his personal struggles as well as the broader hardships of the human condition.
Born in 1819, Courbet was a revolutionary French artist widely considered the father of European Realism.
This art movement is defined by its rejection of romantic portrayals of idealized subjects in favor of raw, unembellished depictions of everyday life.
Courbet created many masterpieces featuring regular people engaged in exhausting activities.
For example, The Stonebreakers shows an old man and a youth dressed in torn and stained clothes breaking and clearing rocks to build a road.
This image reveals the difficulties that laborers faced in their daily lives.

However, critics of his time took a harsh view of Courbet’s work, accusing him of establishing a “cult of ugliness” because he focused on uncomfortable subject matter rather than noble figures or mythological beings.
But Courbet did not take their opinions seriously, famously saying, “Show me an angel and I will paint one.”
What he meant by this was that his goal was to create accurate portrayals of real life.
Whether his subjects were ugly or not did not matter; they were people he had seen and encountered.

sets.name: Unit 05 Reading 4 Edison vs. Tesla: The Shocking Rivalry
sents: In the late 19th century, a rivalry between two brilliant inventors was so intense that it literally sparked electricity.
Thomas Edison and Nikola Tesla fought a bitter battle known as the War of the Currents that determined how electricity would power our world.
In the 1880s, Edison had already established his electrical empire using direct current (DC), a form of electricity that behaves like a steady river, flowing consistently in one direction.
While considered very safe to implement, the DC system had a significant limitation: it couldn’t travel long distances without losing power.
This meant power plants needed to be built every few miles, making it impractical for widespread use, especially in rural areas.
In contrast, Tesla’s system relied on alternating current (AC), which is more like ocean waves flowing back and forth in both directions.
It could send power over long distances with minimal loss, thanks to its ability to be easily transformed to higher voltages.
The difference between Edison and Tesla escalated into a public battle.
Edison was eager to protect the income from his DC patents.
So, he launched an aggressive campaign against AC, claiming it was dangerous.
He even suggested powering the electric chair—an execution device—with AC to demonstrate its fatal risks.
Despite these dramatic tactics, Tesla’s system proved that it was more practical and economical.
At the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago, the host chose Tesla’s more affordable AC system to illuminate the event.
This victory ended the War of the Currents, with AC becoming the standard for power transmission worldwide.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 1 80살의 내가 뭐라고 할까?
sents: Almost everyone has regretted a past decision.
While we can’t completely prevent regrets, Jeff Bezos, the founder of Amazon, believes we can minimize them.
After graduating from college, Bezos began to build an extraordinary career working at various financial firms.
He even became the vice president of one company by the age of 26!
However, Bezos had a bigger dream: to establish his own business.
Bezos sought advice from David E. Shaw, the founder and president of the company where he worked, about this aspiration.

When he explained his plan to quit his job and start an online bookstore, Shaw listened carefully and then told him that it was a good idea, but it would be an even better idea for someone who didn’t already have a promising career.
Then he convinced Bezos to wait 48 hours before making a decision.
During this time, Bezos asked himself whether he would regret choosing this new challenge over stability once he was 80 years old.
The answer was clearly “No,” even if he failed.
Rather, Bezos believed that he would regret not trying something he was passionate about.
This perspective made the difficult decision much easier, and he founded Amazon, which has become incredibly successful.
From that point forward, whenever he faced challenging crossroads, he applied the same approach, which he called the Regret Minimization Framework.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 2 생각 안 한 죄, 사형입니다
sents: Where does evil come from?
According to philosopher Hannah Arendt, evil does not reside solely in society’s worst monsters; it can emerge in anyone whenever thought is absent.
She came to this realization in 1961 while reporting on the trial of Adolf Eichmann.
He was accused of war crimes for organizing the transportation of Jewish people to concentration camps during World War II.
Despite claiming he was merely following orders and bore no personal responsibility, Eichmann was found guilty and sentenced to death.

While Arendt agreed with the verdict, she argued that Eichmann, unlike other Nazis who passionately believed in their horrific ideologies, was a simple administrator who committed evil acts without the intention to cause harm to others.
Arendt coined the phrase “the banality of evil” to describe how ordinary people could commit inhuman acts when they fail to think critically about their actions.

Controversial at the time, her analysis suggested that moral responsibility can be neglected when performing mundane tasks thoughtlessly, which can lead to evil consequences that the offender is unaware of.
In The Life of the Mind, her final work published after her death in 1975, Arendt offers a profound philosophical perspective on thinking and morality.
She defined thinking as a continuous process of self-reflection essential to moral responsibility.
Thus, it is through constant self-questioning that we consider the meaning and purpose of our actions.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 3 어라...? 나 어째서 눈물이...
sents: Sitting by a port in Portugal, you hear someone singing passionately.
Though you can’t understand the words, you notice the emotional depth of the performance.
It fills you with a sense of melancholy and even sadness.
This is fado—a traditional Portuguese music genre.
Originating in the 1830s, fado takes its name from the Portuguese word for fate.
It began in the port city of Lisbon, where sailors embarking on unpredictable journeys would sing about the sorrow of leaving home, the uncertainty of return, and the hope of seeing loved ones again.
A traditional fado performance features a solo singer accompanied by two guitarists.

While one plays the classic guitar, the other plays the Portuguese guitar, a unique pear-shaped instrument with twelve strings arranged in six pairs, which has six more strings than a conventional guitar.
Over time, fado has evolved, with modern performances often incorporating instruments like the bass guitar, saxophone, and piano to increase the complexity of the music.
The themes of hardship and hope, though still central, are now understood through the experiences of contemporary life, such as the loneliness that many residents of modern cities feel.
For nearly two centuries, fado has been a symbol of Portuguese identity and culture.
In recognition of its importance, UNESCO added fado to the Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2011.

sets.name: Unit 06 Reading 4 Dress Well, Feel Well
sents: When you’re feeling down, do you go for a run, call a friend, or play with your dog?
All of these activities can help boost your mood because they trigger the release of dopamine, a chemical linked to happiness.
Interestingly, dopamine is also released when you wear your favorite outfits.
This idea is at the heart of dopamine dressing.
The concept was introduced by fashion psychologist Dawnn Karen, who developed it during the pandemic.
People typically dress for specific purposes, such as to fit in with friends or to follow a workplace dress code.
When the pandemic led to the disappearance of social events and forced many to work from home, Karen recognized the importance of dressing for oneself —wearing clothes that make you feel good.

Karen’s idea draws on the established principles of color therapy, which suggest that certain colors can evoke specific emotions, such as red sparking excitement or blue being associated with calmness.
But dopamine dressing acknowledges that not everyone has conventional color associations; it emphasizes the personal connection a person has with certain outfits.
A cozy sweater gifted by a loved one may bring warmth and comfort, while a pair of bold shoes might make someone feel confident.
Even the texture of clothing, such as the softness of a well-worn hoodie or the sleekness of a silk dress, can arouse positive feelings.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 1 초고층 건물의 저주
sents: Can the construction of skyscrapers serve as an indicator of an economic decline?
That’s what economist Andrew Lawrence believes.
He calls it the Skyscraper Curse.
Going back to 1899, he compared the timing of skyscraper construction plans with major economic cycles, identifying a recurring pattern.
The Chrysler Building, for instance, was initiated in 1928, just before the 1929 stock market crash and the onset of the Great Depression.
Similarly, the Petronas Towers were planned in the early 1990s ahead of the Asian financial crisis, while the Burj Khalifa in Dubai began construction several years before the 2008 global collapse.
The underlying cause of the Skyscraper Curse can be traced to economic cycles driven by monetary policy.
When central banks lower interest rates and increase the money supply, businesses and investors are encouraged to take on more debt and invest in large-scale projects, including skyscrapers.
However, when the economic boom inevitably slows down and interest rates rise, the economy enters a downturn as these massive structures are completed.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 2 잃은 게 아니야, 사실은...
sents: In a tranquil seaside village, an elderly fisherman observed Mia, a young woman, appearing profoundly disheartened.
“What’s troubling you?” the fisherman asked.
Mia sighed and replied, “I feel stuck in unhealthy relationships.
Not only do they exhaust my emotional reserves but I am also entirely uncertain about how to proceed.”
The fisherman bent down and picked up an empty lobster shell.
“When a lobster grows, it has to break free from its old shell.
It becomes vulnerable for a while, but it can’t reach its full size unless it sheds the shell first.”
Mia gazed at the shell, contemplating.
“Just like the lobster, you too may need to let go of relationships that no longer serve you,” the fisherman continued.
“It might feel uncomfortable at first, like being exposed without protection.”
“But that temporary discomfort creates space for something better to grow,” said the old man, picking up a larger shell and handing it to Mia.
“Growth often means leaving something behind, even if it’s difficult.”
Mia nodded, gaining a new perspective.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 3 사실 아무도 원하지 않았다!
sents: On a hot summer day in 1971, social psychologist Jerry Harvey’s father-in-law suggested that the family take a trip to the town of Abilene for lunch.
After they returned home, everyone admitted that they hadn’t really wanted to go in the first place and blamed his father-in-law for suggesting a two-hour drive for a meal that no one enjoyed.
His father-in-law explained that he only suggested it because he thought the family was getting bored staying at home.
This experience became the basis for the Abilene paradox, describing situations where a group pursues actions that contradict individual preferences.
The concept is driven by psychological barriers that prevent honest communication within groups.
One example is action anxiety, which occurs when people feel discomfort at the mere thought of acting on their genuine beliefs.
This anxiety is often amplified by negative fantasies that they might be branded disloyal or blamed for a group’s mistakes, leading to fears of social isolation or harm to their reputation.
As a result, individuals often can’t help withholding minority opinions.
This tendency becomes even stronger when they believe a group consensus has already formed.
The Abilene paradox can be especially unfavorable in organizational settings.
For companies, it prevents the extraction of individual expertise, hindering effective decision-making and slowing innovation.
When employees feel they can’t express their opinions freely, they become disengaged, leading to lower motivation, reduced productivity, and higher turnover.
In the end, they will seek workplaces where open dialogue is encouraged.

sets.name: Unit 07 Reading 4 Study Playlist: Hit or Miss?
sents: You’re sitting at your desk with your textbooks, notes, and highlighters, feeling ready to study hard for your upcoming exams.
Just as you’re about to start, you wonder: should you include music in your review session?
From a neuroscience perspective, incorporating music into learning can serve as a mental endurance booster by maintaining engagement and reducing cognitive fatigue.
Classical or ambient music, in particular, may enhance concentration by providing a structured auditory environment that minimizes external distractions.
Additionally, its structured melodies help learners create associative cues that aid in recall, especially in tasks involving pattern recognition or creative problem-solving.
While music can be a powerful cognitive tool, its effectiveness varies depending on the type of music.
Experts point out songs with lyrics and high-tempo compositions may disrupt reading comprehension by competing for cognitive resources in the brain’s language-processing centers.
Therefore, for music to be a beneficial study aid, learners should select music based on their personal cognitive responses and study needs.
If you have not found the right music yet, starting your study session without any background sounds might not be a bad choice.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 1 페이지 새로고침, 가격도 새로고침
sents: It’s March, and you’re already searching for a flight for your upcoming summer vacation to Hawaii.
Luckily, you find a reasonably priced ticket and immediately press “Buy.”
But when the webpage finishes loading a few seconds later, your jaw drops—the price for the same seat has doubled in the blink of an eye!
This is an example of dynamic pricing.
Dynamic pricing refers to a strategy wherein a product’s price fluctuates in real-time, contingent upon variables such as demand, competitor pricing, and supply levels.
During high-demand periods, such as holidays or vacation seasons, industries like airlines and hotels often raise their prices accordingly to maximize revenue.
However, dynamic pricing is not effective for all products or services.
For instance, Coca-Cola once introduced a vending machine that charged higher prices on hotter days.
But the machines failed to boost revenue because hardly anyone bought a Coke when the price went up.
Did people suddenly stop drinking soft drinks despite the hot weather?
Of course, that was not the case.
Unlike airplane seats, which have a limited supply and few alternatives, beverages like Coca-Cola are available almost everywhere at a fixed price.
So, thirsty customers simply went to a nearby store to quench their thirst with alternative carbonated beverages.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 2 50% 할인 vs 반값 할인
sents: Most people believe they are fairly good at understanding chance.
Yet in reality, humans are surprisingly poor at interpreting probability—even when the math is simple.
Consider a coin tossed several times in a row.
If it lands on heads five times, people begin to feel uneasy.
They assume that tails is now “due.”
However, from a mathematical perspective, each flip is independent and the probability never changes.
The discomfort comes not from incorrect math, but from incorrect intuition.
Truly random events rarely seem arbitrary to the human mind.
The same misunderstanding appears in everyday choices.
When people are told something has a “one in two” chance of happening, it feels different from hearing a “fifty percent” chance, even though both mean the same thing.
Our brains react more strongly to stories and patterns than to numbers, and we search for meaning where none exists.
Because of this, people frequently rely on intuition rather than statistics when making decisions.
So in everyday life, detecting patterns helps humans survive.
However, probability does not follow human expectations.
Randomness naturally includes streaks, clusters, and repetition—features that may seem suspicious but are mathematically normal.
This is why behavior can be influenced by the way information is presented.
For example, people are more willing to try products when success is described as “likely” rather than as a numerical probability, even when the actual chance is identical.
Simply changing the wording makes a risk feel safer or more appealing.
Recognizing the gap between intuition and mathematics can help us make better choices.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 3 멜로디로 치료해 드립니다
sents: When life feels heavy and emotions weigh you down, what do you usually do?
For music lovers, there’s a melodic remedy that transforms melancholy into joy—sunshine pop!
Sunshine pop is a subgenre of pop music that emerged in the mid-1960s in Southern California.
Like the region’s sunny weather, this music sounds warm and bright.
It features joyful, rich vocals and lyrics that usually focus on themes of love and friendship.
Even when lyrics occasionally express feelings of anxiety, they are sung along to an uplifting melody.
Sunshine pop peaked in popularity from the mid to late 1960s, with the Mamas & the Papas being one of the representative bands of this era.
In 1966, the group released a genre-defining song “Monday, Monday,” which combines lyrics about Monday always bringing sadness with an upbeat tone.
This song not only topped the Billboard Hot 100 chart for three consecutive weeks but also won a Grammy for Best Pop Performance by a Group.
Thanks to its catchy harmonies and pleasing sound, this genre remains influential by providing background music in advertisements and movies.

sets.name: Unit 08 Reading 4 Zero Gravity, Zero Defense
sents: Astronauts on the International Space Station (ISS) spend months in an extremely dangerous and stressful environment.
But this is not the only challenge they face; recent research suggests that astronauts may be more susceptible to illnesses such as colds and skin rashes than people on Earth!
The reason for this is that ISS crew members spend an extended period of time in a microgravity environment—one in which objects seem to have no mass because they are in a state of freefall.
Without gravity to constantly pull blood down into the arms and legs, it begins to accumulate in the head.
The body responds by reducing the total amount of blood, which leads to a decline in the number of immune cells that fight infection.
Eventually, the body’s immune system becomes significantly weaker.
So where do the microorganisms that infect astronauts come from?
In some cases, infection occurs due to improperly sterilized equipment or contact with an infected person just before a mission.
Even if these situations are avoided, astronauts can still get sick.
This is because the immune system becomes so weak that latent viruses in the body can be reactivated, triggering a new infection.
Fortunately, this condition is temporary.
Once astronauts return to Earth, their immune systems tend to resume normal function after a few months.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 1 벤치가 부서졌으니 나도 망했군!
sents: Before structured bank systems appeared, merchants in the Middle Ages engaged in money lending and currency exchange from benches in market squares.
If these merchants failed financially, their bench was physically broken so that they could no longer continue trading.
Over time, having a broken bench became synonymous with being unable to pay one’s debts.
This is reflected in the Italian phrase banca rotta, meaning “broken bench,” which later became the root of the English word bankrupt.
As the concept of bankruptcy evolved, legal systems began to formalize the process of debt resolution.
In 15th-century Italy, cities established comprehensive bankruptcy laws to deal with merchants who could not repay their debts.
These laws defined the specific conditions under which merchants could be declared insolvent, creating a structured approach to financial failure.
Then, other European nations eventually adopted similar regulations to handle commercial debt and developed them.
For example, by the 17th century, England had developed a robust legal framework for bankruptcy, distinguishing between fraudulent and unfortunate financial collapse.
In the modern era, declaring bankruptcy is no longer viewed solely as terminal failure.

Rather, it can be understood as a kind of reset button—a sophisticated financial strategy that affords individuals and corporations legal protections, debt restructuring, and genuine opportunities for economic rebirth.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 2 금 가도 걱정 없는 건물이 온다
sents: Built in AD 128, the Pantheon in Rome has a huge concrete dome that has lasted for hundreds of years, showing the strength of concrete and why it is a very popular building material worldwide.
A recent development called bio-concrete may extend the lives of concrete structures even further by enabling them to repair themselves.
While concrete is highly durable, it is still susceptible to damage over time due to variations in temperature and humidity.
Changing environmental conditions create small cracks in the outer surface, through which water can penetrate the interior.
This weakens the concrete, leading to the formation of larger fissures that allow even more moisture to enter.
As the cycle continues, the concrete structure becomes destabilized and may eventually collapse.

In 2006, the Dutch microbiologist Henk Jonkers developed bio-concrete as a potential solution to this problem by adding specific bacteria, such as Bacillus pseudofirmus, and a nutrient known as calcium lactate to the concrete mixture.
The bacteria remain dormant until they encounter water, at which point they activate and begin to feed on the calcium lactate.
A by-product of this process is limestone, a substance that hardens over the course of several weeks to completely seal the crack.
Although self-healing structures seem like something from a science-fiction movie, they are almost a reality.
Bio-concrete has the potential to revolutionize the construction industry by allowing the building of very strong structures that do not need expensive repairs.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 3 소름 돋는데 왜 자꾸 보게 되지?
sents: Imagine standing at the edge of a vast, storm-swept ocean, the horizon stretching endlessly before you.
You feel both insignificant and amazed by the immense power of nature.
This sense captures the essence of the sublime.
At its core, the sublime refers to an aesthetic quality that transcends beauty, evoking awe or a profound sense of grandeur.
In 1757, the Irish philosopher Edmund Burke presented one of the first theories of the sublime in art, arguing that it is the strongest emotion a person could feel.
Whereas beauty evokes memories of familiar, comfortable experiences, the sublime triggers an irresistible sensation of delightful horror.
Throughout history, artists have expressed the sublime in various ways.
The romanticists of the 18th and 19th centuries, in particular, conveyed the majesty and power of nature, depicting towering mountains and violent avalanches.
One example is the German painter Caspar David Friedrich’s work, The Sea of Ice.
It shows the cold landscape of an Arctic ice field, with a tower of jagged ice shards crushing a shipwreck.
Not only is the harsh splendor of the far north revealed, but the unimaginable threat it poses to those who intrude is also revealed.
In contemporary art, abstract expressionists like Mark Rothko sought to evoke the sublime by filling giant canvases with vast fields of color to convey overwhelming human emotions.
Digital and immersive art forms continue this tradition, using technology to create experiences that elicit shock and introspection.

sets.name: Unit 09 Reading 4 Here Comes the Well-Rounded Talent!
sents: Today’s schools are all steamed up—with STEAM!
This innovative pedagogical approach blends Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics to prepare students for an interrelated world.
STEAM education emphasizes the connections between subjects rather than teaching them in isolation.
By integrating the arts with technical subjects, for example, STEAM encourages students to apply artistic creativity and imagination alongside logic and numbers.

When students design a bridge in an engineering project, for example, they don’t simply calculate load capacity; they experiment with different materials and designs to create a bridge that is both structurally sound and visually appealing.
One of the greatest advantages of STEAM education is its emphasis on hands-on, real-world applications.
Instead of passively absorbing theoretical knowledge, students engage in meaningful learning experiences that mirror real-life scenarios.
Students might create digital art to explore design and technology or program robots to see coding in action.
Many of these STEAM projects are carried out in teams, where students collaborate to share ideas and achieve common goals.
Perhaps most importantly, STEAM education fosters students’ adaptability, a crucial skill in today’s job market.

Many industries, from medical technology to entertainment, rely on a combination of science and creativity, proving that STEAM education equips students with the tools they need to thrive in various fields.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 1 다 가져가도 이건 못 가져가
sents: Approximately 200 million individuals of African descent dwell in countries outside of the continent.
They comprise a diaspora, which is a group of people from the same geographic area who create permanent communities in foreign lands.
The origins of the African Diaspora can be traced to two distinct phenomena—slavery and voluntary migration.
From the 16th century to the 19th century, approximately 12 million Africans were forcibly transported to Europe, North America, and South America as part of the transatlantic slave trade.
Despite the extreme hardships these individuals experienced, they retained many aspects of their countries’ cultures, including their cuisine, music, and religious beliefs.
These were passed down from generation to generation, being fundamentally transformed in the process to form the unique cultural identity of their descendants.
Since the termination of the slave trade, millions of Africans have relocated voluntarily to other regions.
Some sought economic or educational opportunities, while others hoped to join family members who already resided abroad.
Regardless of their motivations, these members of the African Diaspora tend to maintain strong cultural, social, and economic connections to their homelands.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 2 75살인데 뇌는 50살이래
sents: Stepping into the jungles of Bolivia is like going back in time.
Here, you’ll find the Tsimane, a tribe of 16,000, who until very recently lived completely traditional lives.
Despite having no access to modern healthcare, they have the lowest rates of cognitive diseases in the world.
For over 20 years, a dedicated research team has been studying this tribe to understand why.
CT scans of Tsimane elders reveal that their brain volume decreases 70 percent more slowly compared to Western populations, significantly reducing their risk of cognitive disorders.
Their Alzheimer’s disease rates are extremely low, occurring in roughly 1% of individuals over 60.
Researchers believe this slower brain deterioration is linked to the tribe’s healthy way of life.
Their traditional living practices of hunting, foraging, and farming provide a nutritious diet of vegetables, fish, and lean meat.
In order to sustain their lifestyle, the Tsimane are highly active, with daily step counts exceeding 15,000, compared to 3,000 steps for Westerners.
And because the tribe is secluded, they have had no exposure to cigarettes, alcohol, or fats used for frying.
These factors have contributed to the average 75-year-old Tsimane having the arteries of a 50-year-old Westerner.
However, the tribe has begun to contact the outside world recently, gaining access to processed foods and ingredients like sugar and oil.
Researchers have already observed an increase in obesity and cholesterol levels, as well as the tribe’s first-ever case of diabetes.
It remains to be seen whether this recent lifestyle shift will increase their rates of cognitive diseases too.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 3 불안한 게 네 탓이 아니야
sents: Does uncertainty stress you out, or do you find it easy to go with the flow?
While this preference may seem like a matter of individual personality, Dutch psychologist Geert Hofstede argued that it is a reflection of culture.
Using data collected from over 30 countries, Hofstede identified uncertainty avoidance (UA) as one of the dimensions that determine the behaviors and values of a culture.
He aimed to understand how societies with varying levels of UA manage risk and ambiguity.
Hofstede classified Greece and Japan as high-UA cultures, where people prioritize security and rely on strict behavioral codes to manage uncertainty.
Greek employees, for instance, favor a structured business environment with clear directives from superiors.
In Japan, lifetime employment and consensus-based decision-making ensure the stability of an organization.
Conversely, in low-UA cultures like that of the United States, people are more open to uncertainty.
They perceive it as a source of freedom and are comfortable in situations without clear guidelines.
For them, ambiguity is an opportunity to forge their own path and innovate.
This mindset promotes a high tolerance for risk and a greater willingness to embrace change.
As globalization increases cultural interactions, these differing approaches to uncertainty management influence international business and social structures.
Companies and individuals alike must learn to balance the need for stability with the benefits of flexibility, adapting their strategies to succeed in a culturally interconnected world.

sets.name: Unit 10 Reading 4 Forever Chemicals, Forever Consequences
sents: “Forever chemicals” may sound romantic, but in reality, they are anything but lovely.
These chemicals, known as PFAS, are characterized by their environmental accumulation.
PFAS combine carbon and fluorine to form virtually indestructible chemical bonds.
Due to their exceptional resistance to heat, grease, and liquids, these chemicals are incorporated into various consumer products, including nonstick pans, waterproof clothing, and food packaging.
However, once these products are discarded, the chemicals accumulate in the environment without naturally breaking down.
Being mobile, they also disperse through the air, soil, and water to remote regions.
Researchers have detected them at the bottom of the ocean and even at the top of Mount Everest!
When PFAS enter lakes and rivers, they build up in the liver, blood, and muscle tissues of fish and other aquatic animals, disrupting hormone regulation, immune function, and reproduction.
As PFAS move up the food chain, they pose a threat to humans who rely on fish from contaminated waters for food.
Recognizing the risks, governments have begun enacting policies to prohibit the use of PFAS in industries such as food packaging and textiles.

While these regulations aim to prevent further contamination, experts argue stronger cleanup efforts and stricter policies are still needed to address pollution that persists in soil and drinking water.
